scenarios.title: Refuse a destructive change
scenarios.tagline: The third revision drops a column. The policy says no, and says so before anything runs.
scenarios.learn: How a policy stops a plan, and where to read what it stopped.
events: # Converged on v2, and the email column holds data.
demo/bin/lab psql "INSERT INTO customers (id, email) VALUES (1, 'a@example.test') RETURNING id, email"
# The next revision removes that column. Someone meant it; the database does not know that.
id bigint NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
# The policy in force allows nothing destructive.
# Publish v3 and point the resource at it.
# It plans, marks the plan destructive, and stops there.
Plan is blocked by destructive-change policy
# The plan exists and says what it is. Destructive is a property of the plan, not a guess.
NAME                                 SCHEMA       FINGERPRINT                                                               STATEMENTS   DESTRUCTIVE   AGE
# And this is the statement the policy refused to run.
destructive  -- Remove columns from table: customers --
ALTER TABLE "customers" DROP COLUMN "email" CASCADE  -- DROP COLUMN removes existing column data
safe  -- WARNING: Dropping column customers.email with CASCADE - This will delete data and dependent objects! --  -- does not remove data or tighten constraints
# The column and its data are still there. A refusal that let it run would not be one.
demo/bin/lab psql "SELECT id, email FROM customers"

checks.claim: exits 0, prints "-  email text NOT NULL"

scenarios.title: Close the drift
scenarios.tagline: Someone changes the database by hand. The operator notices and puts it back.
scenarios.learn: What drift detection reads, and what it does about what it finds.
events: # Converged, and the operator says so with a reason rather than a timestamp.
# Now change the database behind its back, the way an incident does.
demo/bin/lab psql "ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN signed_up_at"
# The column is gone. The declaration still asks for it.
TABLE "orders" CONSTRAINT "fk_orders_customer_id" FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
# Nobody is asked. The operator observes on its interval and closes it.
TABLE "orders" CONSTRAINT "fk_orders_customer_id" FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
# It closed the drift with a plan, the same way it does everything else.
NAME                                 SCHEMA       FINGERPRINT                                                               STATEMENTS   DESTRUCTIVE   AGE

scenarios.title: Fail, then recover
scenarios.tagline: Point it at a database that is not there. It says so, keeps trying, and converges when it is.
scenarios.learn: What a failure looks like in the status, and that recovery needs no intervention beyond the fix.
events: # The same resource, pointed at a database that does not answer.
# It reports the database as unreachable, with a reason a machine can read.
# A failure is an event too, so it is in the record rather than only in a log.
12s         Normal    OperationCompleted   ptahschema/storefront   resolve operation completed
12s         Normal    OperationStarted     ptahschema/storefront   Verify Job ptah-verify-storefront-1e624f0937c69e56 started
9s          Normal    OperationCompleted   ptahschema/storefront   verify operation completed
9s          Normal    OperationStarted     ptahschema/storefront   Observe Job ptah-observe-storefront-3e6c76385e25dc68 started
2s          Warning   OperationFailed      ptahschema/storefront   child_exit: ptah exited with code 2
# No credential in any of it. This is the whole status the operator wrote.
kubectl -n "$NAMESPACE" get ptahschema storefront -o json | jq -r '.status | tostring' | head -c 400
# Now fix the one thing that was wrong.
# It retries on its own interval and converges. Nothing was restarted by hand.

scenarios.title: Apply a schema
scenarios.tagline: Publish a schema as an artifact, point the operator at it, and watch it converge.
scenarios.learn: What the operator does between a desired state and a database, and how it says it is done.
events: # The desired state is SQL. This is the whole of it.
id bigint NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
# Publish it. The push runs in the cluster, as the Ptah build the operator will run.
DIGEST=$(demo/bin/lab publish v1) && echo "$DIGEST" | tee demo/.lab/digest
# That is the command it ran. A reference, a dialect, and the file it read.
# The resource names the artifact by digest, and the credentials by Secret.
demo/bin/lab manifest storefront "$(cat demo/.lab/digest)" | tee demo/.lab/storefront.yaml
# The desired state of one database, as a Kubernetes resource.
# Nothing here is a credential. The database URL and the registry password are
# named, and read by the operator from Secrets this namespace holds; what the
# resource carries is which artifact, which database, and what the operator is
# allowed to do about the difference.
# Every resource that can reach this physical database, through any alias
# or credential, has to use this exact key. It is how two of them are kept
# A digest, not a tag: what was reviewed is what runs.
# Apply it. Nothing else is typed after this; the operator does the rest.
# Resolve, verify, observe, plan, apply, and prove. Each is a condition.
# Applying says False, reason JobCompleted. A finished Job is not a converged database.
InSync: A stable scoped plan proves convergence
Applying: Apply Job completed; convergence observation is pending
# The plan it derived, and the SQL that plan carried.
NAME                                 SCHEMA       FINGERPRINT                                                               STATEMENTS   DESTRUCTIVE   AGE
# The SQL lives in an immutable ConfigMap, not in a status field or a log line.

checks.claim: exits 0, prints "kind: PtahSchema", prints "ociRef: oci://", prints "urlFrom", never prints "password:"
ptahschema/storefront: Ready=True (InSync), status.phase=InSync, status.applied.artifactDigest is set

scenarios.title: Stand up the lab
scenarios.tagline: A four-node kind cluster, the chart from a package, and every image pinned by digest.
scenarios.learn: What the other runs are against, and how to tell an install that finished from one that started.
events: # The lab is one cluster, built from the versions this repository declares.
# The operator runs in its own namespace, two replicas, one leader.
# Available means the install finished. The image is a digest, so one exact build runs.
# Three resources -- the desired state, the plan, and the decision that lets it run.
# The namespace it works in. Credentials are Secrets; the policy cannot be edited.

checks.claim: exits 0, prints "kubernetes", prints "kind", prints "operator", prints "executor", prints "ptah"
exits 0, prints "demo-database", prints "demo-registry", prints "demo-verification-policy", never prints "password"

scenarios.title: Approve a plan
scenarios.tagline: With apply set to OnApproval, nothing runs until a person approves that exact plan.
scenarios.learn: What an approval is bound to, and how much of that binding you never type.
events: # Same resource, one field different -- apply is OnApproval, which is the default.
APPLY=OnApproval demo/bin/lab manifest storefront "$(cat demo/.lab/digest)" | tee demo/.lab/storefront.yaml
# The desired state of one database, as a Kubernetes resource.
# Nothing here is a credential. The database URL and the registry password are
# named, and read by the operator from Secrets this namespace holds; what the
# resource carries is which artifact, which database, and what the operator is
# allowed to do about the difference.
# Every resource that can reach this physical database, through any alias
# or credential, has to use this exact key. It is how two of them are kept
# A digest, not a tag: what was reviewed is what runs.
# Apply it, and the operator plans but stops.
# It has a plan and it is waiting. The database has not been touched.
Create an approval bound to the current plan fingerprint
# Nothing was created. This is what waiting looks like from the database.
# Read the plan before approving it. This is what would run.
# An approval names the schema, the plan, and the fingerprint of that plan.
kubectl -n "$NAMESPACE" get ptahschema storefront -o json > demo/.lab/schema.json
# Create it. The webhook stamps who you are and binds the rest of the plan's identity.
# None of this was typed. The webhook read it off the plan being approved.
# With the decision recorded, the plan runs and convergence is proved.
# It was dispatched once, and is already stale. Retiring a used approval shows why.

checks.claim: exits 0, prints "Did not find any relations"
ptahschemaapproval/storefront-v1: spec.approver.username is set, spec.artifactDigest is set, spec.executorImage is set, spec.mutationRequestUID is set

scenarios.title: Change the schema
scenarios.tagline: A second revision, a new digest, and the difference applied as one plan.
scenarios.learn: How a change reaches a database, and why the plan is the thing to review.
events: # Where it starts -- one table, converged.
# The next revision adds a column and a table that references the first.
id bigint NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
+  id bigint NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
+  customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
# Publish it. A different artifact, so a different digest.
# Point the same resource at the new digest. One field changes.
# A new plan, against the database as it actually is rather than as v1 left it.
NAME                                 SCHEMA       FINGERPRINT                                                               STATEMENTS   DESTRUCTIVE   AGE
# The SQL it applied. An ALTER and a CREATE, not a second CREATE TABLE customers.
ALTER TABLE "orders" ADD CONSTRAINT "fk_orders_customer_id" FOREIGN KEY ("customer_id") REFERENCES "customers"("id")
# And the database has both, with the foreign key the declaration asked for.

checks.claim: exits 0, prints "+  signed_up_at timestamptz", prints "+CREATE TABLE orders"

scenarios.title: Retire a used approval
scenarios.tagline: An approval describes one plan against one observed state. Applying it moves that state.
scenarios.learn: Why a signature cannot authorize twice, and what the operator does with one that no longer fits.
events: # A plan is waiting for a decision, and it is named by its fingerprint.
# Approve it, bound to that schema, that plan and that fingerprint.
kubectl -n "$NAMESPACE" get ptahschema storefront -o json > demo/.lab/schema.json
# It converges, and the approval records that it was the one dispatched.
# And already stale. It described a plan against the database before the apply.
The approved plan no longer matches the current database state
# So it cannot authorize a second time. Change the desired state and see.
# A new plan, and the operator waits again. Nothing carries over.
# And the change nobody approved has not run.

scenarios.title: Suspend and resume
scenarios.tagline: One field stops reconciliation without deleting anything, and resuming picks up where it stopped.
scenarios.learn: How to take a database out of the operator's hands during an incident, and give it back.
events: # Suspend it. One boolean, and the resource stays exactly where it is.
# The operator says it is suspended, with the reason on the condition.
# Now publish a change it would otherwise pick up, and point the resource at it.
# Nothing happens, which is the point. The database is untouched.
# Resume, and it starts from what is actually there rather than from what it remembered.
# It plans against the live database and converges on the revision it was given.
